Saturation numbers of K3∨PkK_{3}\vee P_{k}

Huaqin Li, Lihua You*, Xiaoxue Zhang

School of Mathematical Sciences
South China Normal University, Guangzhou, 510631, P. R. China
2024022055@m.scnu.edu.cn, ylhua@scnu.edu.cn, zhang_xx1209@163.com

Abstract: A graph GG is said to be HH-saturated if GG contains no copy of HH, but G+eG+e contains a copy of HH for any edge ee of G¯\overline{G}. The saturation number of HH, denoted by sat⁡(n,H)\mathrm{sat}(n,H), is the minimum number of edges among all HH-saturated graphs of order nn. In this paper, we investigate the saturation number of K3∨PkK_{3}\vee P_{k} for k≥3k\geq 3 and show that sat⁡(n,K3∨Pk)=3​n−6+sat⁡(n−3,Pk)\mathrm{sat}(n,K_{3}\vee P_{k})=3n-6+\mathrm{sat}(n-3,P_{k}) holds for all n≥ak+3n\geq a_{k}+3 and k≥3k\geq 3, which verifies the conjecture [Discrete Appl. Math, 394(2026) 62-80] on sat⁡(n,Ks∨Pk)\mathrm{sat}(n,K_{s}\vee P_{k}) is true for the case s=3s=3, where ak=ka_{k}=k for 3≤k≤53\leq k\leq 5, ak=3⋅2t−1−2a_{k}=3\cdot 2^{t-1}-2 for k=2​t≥6k=2t\geq 6, and ak=2t+1−2a_{k}=2^{t+1}-2 for k=2​t+1≥7k=2t+1\geq 7.

Keywords: Saturation number; Saturation graph; Minimal

1 Introduction

Throughout this paper, we only consider simple, finite, and undirected graphs.

Let G=(V⁡(G),E⁡(G))G=(V(G),E(G)) be a graph with vertex set V⁡(G)V(G) and edge set E⁡(G)E(G). The order of GG is |V⁡(G)||V(G)| and the size of GG is |E⁡(G)||E(G)|. A path, complete graph, or cycle of order nn is denoted by PnP_{n}, KnK_{n} or CnC_{n}, respectively. For a vertex u∈V⁡(G)u\in V(G), the set of neighbors of uu in GG is denoted by NG​(u)N_{G}(u), dG​(u)=|NG​(u)|d_{G}(u)=|N_{G}(u)| is the degree of uu in GG, and NG​[u]=NG​(u)∪{u}N_{G}[u]=N_{G}(u)\cup\{u\} is the closed neighborhood of uu in GG. For u,v∈V⁡(G)u,v\in V(G), the distance between uu and vv is the length of the shortest path connecting uu and vv in GG, and is denoted by dG​(u,v)d_{G}(u,v). The diameter of GG is the greatest distance between two vertices of GG, denoted by diam⁡(G)\operatorname{diam}(G). Let δ⁡(G)\delta(G) and Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G) be the minimum degree and maximum degree of vertices in GG, respectively. When no ambiguity arises, we use N⁡(u)N(u), d⁡(u)d(u), N⁡[u]N[u], d⁡(u,v)d(u,v), δ\delta and Δ\Delta instead of NG​(u)N_{G}(u), dG​(u)d_{G}(u), NG​[u]N_{G}[u], dG​(u,v)d_{G}(u,v), δ⁡(G)\delta(G) and Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G), respectively. A vertex of degree zero is called an isolated vertex. An independent set in a graph is a set of vertices no two of which are adjacent. For X⊆V⁡(G)X\subseteq V(G), we use G⁡[X]G[X] to denote the subgraph of GG induced by XX. For X⊆V⁡(G)X\subseteq V(G) and Y⊆V⁡(G)∖XY\subseteq V(G)\setminus X, EG​[X,Y]E_{G}[X,Y] is the set of edges of GG between XX and YY, denoted simply by E⁡[X,Y]E[X,Y]. The union of two graphs G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} is the graph G1∪G2G_{1}\cup G_{2} with vertex set V⁡(G1)∪V⁡(G2)V(G_{1})\cup V(G_{2}) and edge set E⁡(G1)∪E⁡(G2)E(G_{1})\cup E(G_{2}). The join of graphs G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} is obtained from G1∪G2G_{1}\cup G_{2} by joining each vertex of G1G_{1} to each vertex of G2G_{2}, denoted by G1∨G2G_{1}\vee G_{2}.

A graph HH is called a subgraph of GG if V⁡(H)⊆V⁡(G)V(H)\subseteq V(G) and E⁡(H)⊆E⁡(G)E(H)\subseteq E(G). A copy of HH in GG is a subgraph of GG which is isomorphic to HH. A graph GG is called HH-saturated if GG contains no copy of HH, but G+eG+e contains a copy of HH for any edge e∈E⁡(G¯)e\in E(\overline{G}). The saturation number of HH, denoted by sat⁡(n,H)\operatorname{sat}(n,H), is the minimum number of edges among all HH-saturated graphs of order nn. If GG is an HH-saturated graph with sat⁡(n,H)\operatorname{sat}(n,H) edges, we say GG is a minimal HH-saturated graph.

The concept of the saturation number was introduced by Erdős, Hajnal, and Moon  [11] in 1964. They established the exact value for complete graphs as sat⁡(n,Kp)=(p−2)​(n−p+2)+(p−22)\operatorname{sat}(n,K_{p})=(p-2)(n-p+2)+\binom{p-2}{2} and characterized Kp−2∨K¯n−p+2K_{p-2}\vee\overline{K}_{n-p+2} as the unique minimal saturated graph. Since then, many exact saturation numbers are now known. These include stars, paths, and matchings [22]; cycles [7, 8, 15, 17, 23, 24, 29]; complete bipartite and multipartite graphs [1, 9, 18, 21]; nearly complete graphs [13]; linear forests [3, 5, 12]; vertex-disjoint cliques [4, 14, 30]; regular saturated graphs [16, 28]; hypergraphs [25]; books and generalized books [6] and so on. More results can be found in [10].

The join of graphs is an important binary operation in graph theory, and the saturation numbers concerning the joins of certain specific graphs have attracted considerable attention. In 2024, Hu, Luo, and Peng [20] showed that if DD is a graph without isolated vertices, then sat⁡(n,Ks∨D)=(s2)+s⁡(n−s)+sat⁡(n−s,D)\operatorname{sat}(n,K_{s}\vee D)=\binom{s}{2}+s(n-s)+\operatorname{sat}(n-s,D) holds when s≥1s\geq 1 and n≥3​s2−s+2​sat⁡(n−s,D)+1n\geq 3s^{2}-s+2\operatorname{sat}(n-s,D)+1. However, Qiu, He, Lu, and Xu [26] pointed out that under the condition n≥3​s2−s+2​sat⁡(n−s,D)+1n\geq 3s^{2}-s+2\operatorname{sat}(n-s,D)+1, the graph DD must contain a K2K_{2}. Therefore, it is interested to investigate the saturation numbers when DD does not contain a K2K_{2}. Qiu, He, Lu, and Xu [26] proved that sat⁡(n,K1∨Ck)=n−1+sat⁡(n−1,Ck)\operatorname{sat}(n,K_{1}\vee C_{k})=n-1+\operatorname{sat}(n-1,C_{k}) for k≥8k\geq 8 and n≥56​k3n\geq 56k^{3}. When k=4k=4, Song, Hu, Ji, and Cui [27] proved that sat⁡(n,K1∨C4)=n−1+sat⁡(n−1,C4)\operatorname{sat}(n,K_{1}\vee C_{4})=n-1+\operatorname{sat}(n-1,C_{4}) for n≥6n\geq 6. In 2025, Hu, Ji, and Cui [19] proved that sat⁡(n,K1∨Pk)=n−1+sat⁡(n−1,Pk)\operatorname{sat}(n,K_{1}\vee P_{k})=n-1+\operatorname{sat}(n-1,P_{k}) for k≥5k\geq 5 and sufficiently large nn. Furthermore, in 2026, Zhang, You, and Zhao [31] proved that sat⁡(n,K2∨Pk)=2​n−3+sat⁡(n−2,Pk)\operatorname{sat}(n,K_{2}\vee P_{k})=2n-3+\operatorname{sat}(n-2,P_{k}) for n≥ak+2n\geq a_{k}+2 and k≥3k\geq 3, and proposed a conjecture about sat⁡(n,Ks∨Pk)\operatorname{sat}(n,K_{s}\vee P_{k}) as follows.

Conjecture 1.1 ([31]).

Let k,s≥3k,s\geq 3, n≥ak+sn\geq a_{k}+s, where

ak={k,if ​3≤k≤5;3⋅2t−1−2,if ​k≥6​ and ​k=2​t;2t+1−2,if ​k≥7​ and ​k=2​t+1.a_{k}=\begin{cases}k,&\text{if }3\leq k\leq 5;\\ 3\cdot 2^{t-1}-2,&\text{if }k\geq 6\text{ and }k=2t;\\ 2^{t+1}-2,&\text{if }k\geq 7\text{ and }k=2t+1.\end{cases} (1.1)

Then sat⁡(n,Ks∨Pk)=(s2)+s⁡(n−s)+sat⁡(n−s,Pk)\operatorname{sat}(n,K_{s}\vee P_{k})=\binom{s}{2}+s(n-s)+\operatorname{sat}(n-s,P_{k}).

In this paper, we improve upon the methods used to determine sat⁡(n,K2∨Pk)\operatorname{sat}(n,K_{2}\vee P_{k}) [31] and verify Conjecture 1.1 is true for the case s=3s=3. The following is our main result.

Theorem 1.2.

Let k≥3k\geq 3, n≥ak+3n\geq a_{k}+3, where aka_{k} is defined as (1.1). Then

sat⁡(n,K3∨Pk)=3​n−6+sat⁡(n−3,Pk)={⌊7​n−152⌋,if ​k=3;7​n−152,if ​k=4,n​ is odd;7​n−122,if ​k=4,n​ is even;⌈23​n−556⌉,if ​k=5;4​n−9−⌊n−3ak⌋,if ​k≥6.\operatorname{sat}(n,K_{3}\vee P_{k})=3n-6+\operatorname{sat}(n-3,P_{k})=\begin{cases}\left\lfloor\frac{7n-15}{2}\right\rfloor,&\text{if }k=3;\\ \frac{7n-15}{2},&\text{if }k=4,n\text{ is odd};\\ \frac{7n-12}{2},&\text{if }k=4,n\text{ is even};\\ \left\lceil\frac{23n-55}{6}\right\rceil,&\text{if }k=5;\\ 4n-9-\left\lfloor\frac{n-3}{a_{k}}\right\rfloor,&\text{if }k\geq 6.\end{cases} (1.2)

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we present some known results that are useful for the proof. In Section 3, we prove Theorem 1.2. In Section 4, we conclude this paper.

2 Preliminaries

In this section, we present some results and notation that will be used later. For convenience, we refer to K3K_{3} and PkP_{k} as the center and path part of K3∨PkK_{3}\vee P_{k}, respectively, and use C⁡(K3∨Pk)C(K_{3}\vee P_{k}) and P​P​(K3∨Pk)PP(K_{3}\vee P_{k}) to denote the sets of vertices in the center and the path part of K3∨PkK_{3}\vee P_{k}, respectively.

Theorem 2.1 ([22]).

Let k≥3k\geq 3 and aka_{k} be defined as (1.1). Then we have
(i) sat⁡(n,P3)=⌊n2⌋\operatorname{sat}(n,P_{3})=\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor for n≥3n\geq 3.
(ii) sat⁡(n,P4)={n2,for ​n≥4,n​ is even;n+32,for ​n≥5,n​ is odd.\operatorname{sat}(n,P_{4})=\begin{cases}\frac{n}{2},&\text{for }n\geq 4,n\text{ is even};\\ \frac{n+3}{2},&\text{for }n\geq 5,n\text{ is odd}.\end{cases}
(iii) sat⁡(n,P5)=⌈5​n−46⌉\operatorname{sat}(n,P_{5})=\left\lceil\frac{5n-4}{6}\right\rceil for n≥5n\geq 5.
(iv) sat⁡(n,Pk)=n−⌊nak⌋\operatorname{sat}(n,P_{k})=n-\left\lfloor\frac{n}{a_{k}}\right\rfloor for n≥akn\geq a_{k} and k≥6k\geq 6.

Theorem 2.2 ([31]).

Let k≥3k\geq 3, n≥ak+2n\geq a_{k}+2, where aka_{k} is defined as (1.1). Then we have sat​(n,K2∨Pk)=2​n−3+sat​(n−2,Pk)\text{sat}(n,K_{2}\vee P_{k})=2n-3+\text{sat}(n-2,P_{k}).

Proposition 2.3 ([31]).

For n≥k+sn\geq k+s and k,s≥3k,s\geq 3, sat​(n,Ks∨Pk)≤(s2)+s⁡(n−s)+sat​(n−s,Pk)\text{sat}(n,K_{s}\vee P_{k})\leq\binom{s}{2}+s(n-s)+\text{sat}(n-s,P_{k}).

Proposition 2.4 ([31]).

Let GG be a K1∨HK_{1}\vee H-saturated graph of order nn. If Δ⁡(G)=n−1\Delta(G)=n-1, then |E⁡(G)|≥n−1+sat​(n−1,H)|E(G)|\geq n-1+\text{sat}(n-1,H), the equality holds if and only if G≅K1∨FG\cong K_{1}\vee F, where FF is a minimal HH-saturated graph of order n−1n-1.

Proposition 2.5.

Let GG be a Ks∨PkK_{s}\vee P_{k}-saturated graph with s≥2,k≥3s\geq 2,k\geq 3, x,y∈V⁡(G)x,y\in V(G), x​y∉E⁡(G)xy\notin E(G), and QQ be a copy of Ks∨PkK_{s}\vee P_{k} in G+x​yG+xy. Then we have
(1) there exists V1⊆V⁡(G)V_{1}\subseteq V(G), such that {x,y}∪C⁡(Q)⊆V1\{x,y\}\cup C(Q)\subseteq V_{1}, and G⁡[V1]+x​y≅Ks+2G[V_{1}]+xy\cong K_{s+2}.
(2) there exist at least s paths of length 22 from xx to yy in GG.
(3) d​i​a​m​(G)=2diam(G)=2 and δ⁡(G)≥s\delta(G)\geq s.
(4) C⁡(Q)⊆{x,y}∪(N⁡(x)∩N⁡(y))C(Q)\subseteq\{x,y\}\cup(N(x)\cap N(y)).

Proof. Let

V1={C⁡(Q)∪{z1,z2}, where ​z1,z2∈P​P​(Q),z1​z2∈E⁡(Q),if ​x,y∈C⁡(Q);C⁡(Q)∪{y,z}, where ​z∈P​P​(Q)∩N⁡(y),if x∈C(Q),y∈PP(Q);C⁡(Q)∪{x,y},if ​x,y∈P​P​(Q).V_{1}=\begin{cases}C(Q)\cup\{z_{1},z_{2}\},\text{ where }z_{1},z_{2}\in PP(Q),z_{1}z_{2}\in E(Q),&\text{if }x,y\in C(Q);\\ C(Q)\cup\{y,z\},\text{ where }z\in PP(Q)\cap N(y),&\text{if }x\in C(Q),y\in PP(Q);\\ C(Q)\cup\{x,y\},&\text{if }x,y\in PP(Q).\\ \end{cases}

Clearly, {x,y}∪C⁡(Q)⊆V1⊆V⁡(G)\{x,y\}\cup C(Q)\subseteq V_{1}\subseteq V(G) and G⁡[V1]+x​y≅Ks+2G[V_{1}]+xy\cong K_{s+2}, and thus (1) holds. By (1) and direct checking, (2), (3), and (4) hold immediately. □\square

3 Proof of Theorem 1.2

For the cases k=1,2k=1,2, we note that K3∨P1≅K4K_{3}\vee P_{1}\cong K_{4} and K3∨P2≅K5K_{3}\vee P_{2}\cong K_{5}, the results for which have already been established in [11]. In this section, we prove Theorem 1.2.

Proof of Theorem 1.2. Let GG be a K3∨PkK_{3}\vee P_{k}-saturated graph with k≥3k\geq 3 of order nn. In order to show (1.2), by Theorem 2.1 and Proposition 2.3, we only need to show

|E⁡(G)|≥3​n−6+sat⁡(n−3,Pk).|E(G)|\geq 3n-6+\operatorname{sat}(n-3,P_{k}). (3.1)

Then δ≥3\delta\geq 3 and |E⁡[{u},N⁡(v)]|≠∅|E[\{u\},N(v)]|\neq\emptyset for any u∈Uu\in U by (3) of Proposition 2.5 and s=3s=3.

For any vi∈N⁡(v)v_{i}\in N(v), we call viv_{i} a K3K_{3}-vertex if there exist v′,v′′∈N⁡(v)v^{\prime},v^{\prime\prime}\in N(v) such that G⁡[{vi,v′,v′′}]≅K3G[\{v_{i},v^{\prime},v^{\prime\prime}\}]\cong K_{3}. Otherwise, we call viv_{i} a non-K3K_{3}-vertex.

Let VK3V_{K_{3}} and VN​K3V_{NK_{3}} be the sets of all K3K_{3}-vertices and all non-K3K_{3}-vertices in N⁡(v)N(v), respectively, and let G⁡[VK3]=GK3G[V_{K_{3}}]=G_{K_{3}}, and G⁡[VN​K3]=GN​K3G[V_{NK_{3}}]=G_{NK_{3}}. Then VK3∩VN​K3=∅V_{K_{3}}\cap V_{NK_{3}}=\emptyset, and VK3∪VN​K3=N⁡(v)V_{K_{3}}\cup V_{NK_{3}}=N(v).

For any u∈Uu\in U, {t1,t2,…,tp}⊆{1,2,…,δ}\{t_{1},t_{2},\dots,t_{p}\}\subseteq\{1,2,\dots,\delta\}, we define

Up={u∈U∣|N⁡(u)∩N⁡(v)|=p},U≥p=⋃q=pδUq,U_{p}=\{u\in U\mid|N(u)\cap N(v)|=p\},\quad U_{\geq p}=\bigcup_{q=p}^{\delta}U_{q},
Xt1t2⋯tp={u∣u∈Up∩N(vt1)∩N(vt2)∩⋯∩N(vtp)}.X_{t_{1}t_{2}\cdots t_{p}}=\{u\mid u\in U_{p}\cap N(v_{t_{1}})\cap N(v_{t_{2}})\cap\cdots\cap N(v_{t_{p}})\}.

|E⁡(G)|=|E⁡(G⁡[N⁡[v]])|+∑p=3δp​|Up|+|E⁡(G⁡[U])|.\displaystyle|E(G)|=|E(G[N[v]])|+\sum_{p=3}^{\delta}p|U_{p}|+|E(G[U])|.\text{ } (3.2)
Claim 1.

Let 3≤p≤δ3\leq p\leq\delta. The following hold.
(1) If G⁡[{vt1,vt2,…,vtp}]G[\{v_{t_{1}},v_{t_{2}},\dots,v_{t_{p}}\}] contains no copy of K3K_{3}, where {t1,t2,…,tp}⊆{1,2,…,δ}\{t_{1},t_{2},\dots,t_{p}\}\subseteq\{1,2,\dots,\delta\}, then Xt1​…​tp=∅X_{t_{1}\dots t_{p}}=\emptyset.

Claim 2.

Let vi∈N⁡(v)v_{i}\in N(v). If G⁡[N⁡(v)∖{vi}]G[N(v)\setminus\{v_{i}\}] contains no copy of K3K_{3} and dG⁡[N⁡(v)]​(vi)=δ−1d_{G[N(v)]}(v_{i})=\delta-1, then d⁡(vi)=n−1d(v_{i})=n-1.

Proof of Claim 2. We show d⁡(vi)=n−1d(v_{i})=n-1 by considering U=∅U=\emptyset and U≠∅U\neq\emptyset.

4 Conclusion

In this paper, we investigate the saturation number of K3∨PkK_{3}\vee P_{k} for k≥3k\geq 3 and n≥ak+3n\geq a_{k}+3 and show Theorem 1.2 holds by showing (3.1) holds. In the proof, we adapt the vertex-partition method of [31], introduce the sets VK3V_{K_{3}}, VN​K3V_{NK_{3}}, U≥pU_{\geq p} to obtain a further refinement, define the notation GK3G_{K_{3}}, GN​K3G_{NK_{3}}, r=|C⁡(Q)∩U|r=|C(Q)\cap U| and so on, and obtain the lower bound on |E⁡(G)||E(G)| given by a simpler expression.

Furthermore, natural problems are to characterize all minimal (K3∨Pk)(K_{3}\vee P_{k})- saturated graphs and to investigate whether analogous local reductions can determine sat⁡(n,Ks∨Pk)\operatorname{sat}(n,K_{s}\vee P_{k}) for larger fixed values of ss[31].
